title: Achaemenides apud Polyphemum
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas comes up out of the Stygian halls into the Euboean city, makes the customary offerings, and lands on a shore that does not yet carry his nurse's name. There Macareus, a companion of Ulysses who has stayed behind, recognises Achaemenides — the man once left among the crags of Aetna — and asks what chance or god keeps him alive and why a Greek is riding in a barbarian ship. Achaemenides answers with an oath of gratitude to Aeneas and then with what he watched Polyphemus do: the blinded giant hurling rocks after the escaping ship, then groping his way round the mountain, wishing aloud for another Greek to eat, and eating men; and he ends by asking Macareus for his own story.
advisory: This part dwells on the Cyclops eating men — flesh, bones with their white marrow, half-living limbs — and on his wish to do it again to another Greek, whose blood would flood his throat and whose crushed limbs would twitch under his teeth; Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Talia convexum per iter memorante Sibylla
sedibus Euboicam Stygiis emergit in urbem
Troius Aeneas sacrisque ex more litatis
litora adit nondum nutricis habentia nomen.
sentences.l: With the Sibyl relating such things along the vaulted road, Trojan Aeneas emerges from the Stygian dwellings into the Euboean city, and, the rites having been duly offered after the custom, he approaches shores not yet holding the name of his nurse.
sentences.i: So the Sibyl told her story as they climbed the vaulted road, and Trojan Aeneas came up out of the dwellings of the Styx into the city of the Euboeans; then, the offerings made and accepted as custom required, he came to a shore that did not yet bear his nurse's name.
sentences.n: The part opens on two ablative absolutes, one at each end: Talia ... memorante Sibylla, “with the Sibyl relating such things”, and sacris ex more litatis, “with the rites duly offered”. Latin can hang a whole clause on a noun and a participle in this way, and English has to unpack each into “with X doing Y” or “when X had been done”. litare is not simply to sacrifice but to sacrifice successfully — to get the favourable answer — so the phrase says the offerings were accepted, not merely made. sedibus Stygiis is a bare ablative of separation with no preposition, “from the Stygian dwellings”. emergit is a historic present, and it keeps the coming-up-out-of-the-earth in front of the reader. nondum, “not yet”, is doing the real work of the last line: the shore is pointed at before it has the name it will carry, and the nurse herself is not named here at all.

sentences.t:
Hic quoque substiterat per taedia longa laborum
Neritius Macareus, comes experientis Ulixei;
sentences.l: Here too had stayed behind, through the long weariness of their labours, Neritian Macareus, companion of enterprising Ulysses;
sentences.i: Here too Macareus of Neritos had dropped out, worn down by the long tedium of their hardships — a companion of Ulysses the enterprising;
sentences.n: Hic is the adverb “here”, of this shore, not the pronoun “this man”; substiterat is pluperfect, so he had already stopped here before Aeneas arrived. Neritius is from Neritos, a mountain of Ithaca, and stands for “Ithacan”. experiens is the participle of experior used as an adjective: the man who tries things, who puts himself to the test. Ulixei is a Greek-flavoured genitive of Ulixes. Magnus prints per taedia longa, “through the long weariness”, which gives the weariness as the cause of his stopping; some editions print post, “after the long weariness”, which makes it only the time.

sentences.t:
desertum quondam mediis e rupibus Aetnae
noscit Achaemeniden improvisoque repertum
vivere miratus “qui de casusve deusve
servat, Achaemenide?
sentences.l: He recognises Achaemenides, once abandoned out of the middle crags of Aetna, and marvelling that the man, unexpectedly found, was alive: “What chance or what god preserves you, Achaemenides?
sentences.i: He knows Achaemenides, the man once left behind among the crags of Aetna, and he marvels to find him living and unlooked-for: “What chance or what god is keeping you alive, Achaemenides?
sentences.n: noscit is a historic present. miratus is a deponent perfect participle, active in meaning — “having marvelled”, not “having been marvelled at” — and it governs the accusative and infinitive repertum ... vivere, “that the man, found, was alive”. improviso is an adverbial ablative, “unexpectedly”. No verb of speaking is supplied before the quotation opens; inquit arrives only after the first question. qui here is the interrogative adjective, an older form beside quis: “what chance, what god”. Two things to say about the text as Magnus prints it. First, the printed de cannot be construed: de is a preposition taking the ablative and there is nothing in the ablative for it to govern, while servat is transitive and stands without an object; the second witness reads te, “you”, which supplies exactly the object the syntax wants, and the translation above supplies that sense — nothing has been altered in the line as printed. Second, Magnus prints e with mediis rupibus, “out of the middle crags”, a preposition that sits oddly with desertum, since Achaemenides was left in the crags rather than out of them; some editions print qui in its place, which leaves mediis rupibus as a plain ablative of place, “among the crags”, and turns the whole sentence into a relative clause hanging on Macareus. The literal above keeps the printed preposition, “out of the middle crags”; the idiomatic gives the sense the passage requires either way, “among the crags”.

sentences.t:
cur” inquit “barbara Graium
prora vehit?
sentences.l: “Why,” he says, “does a barbarian prow carry a Greek?
sentences.i: “Why,” he says, “is a barbarian ship carrying a Greek aboard?
sentences.n: inquit is dropped inside the quotation rather than standing in front of it — inside is the position Latin regularly gives it. prora, the prow, stands for the whole ship. barbarus is the Greek word for a non-Greek, and Macareus uses it of the people who have taken Achaemenides aboard: from a Greek deck the Trojans are the foreigners, and the contempt in the word is his, not the poem's. Graium is best taken as the accusative singular of Graius, “a Greek”, the object of vehit; the same form is also the ordinary poetic genitive plural, “of the Greeks”, but that reading leaves vehit with nothing to carry.

sentences.t: petitur vestra quae terra carina?”
sentences.l: What land is being sought by your keel?”
sentences.i: What land is your ship making for?”
sentences.n: petitur is passive and terra is its subject: Latin says “what land is being sought”, where English would rather say “what land are you making for”. vestra carina is an ablative of the instrument — the ship does the seeking. quae is the interrogative adjective agreeing with terra and stands next to it; vestra belongs with carina at the end of the line, so that phrase is split around quae terra. prora in the first half of 164 and carina at its end are both parts of a ship standing for the whole of it, and both fall inside this one line.

sentences.t:
Talia quaerenti iam non hirsutus amictu,
iam suus et spinis conserto tegmine nullis,
fatur Achaemenides:
sentences.l: To the man asking such things Achaemenides speaks, now not shaggy as to his cloak, now his own, and with his covering fastened together by no thorns:
sentences.i: To these questions Achaemenides makes answer — no longer shaggy in his wrappings, his own man again, his clothing held together by no thorns:
sentences.n: quaerenti is a participle used as a noun in the dative, “to the one asking”, so Macareus does not have to be named again. hirsutus amictu has amictu as an ablative of respect, “shaggy in respect of his covering”: the ablative names the thing an adjective is true of, and English has to say “as to” or “in”. iam suus, “now his own”, is the shortest way Latin has of saying that he belongs to himself again. spinis conserto tegmine nullis is an ablative absolute, “his covering fastened together by no thorns”, with nullis thrown out to the end of 166, as far from spinis as the line allows; it says by negation what his clothing was when Ulysses left him. fatur is deponent, active in meaning, and it is a solemn, epic verb of speaking.

sentences.t:
“Iterum Polyphemon et illos
adspiciam fluidos humano sanguine rictus,
hac mihi si potior domus est Ithacique carina,
si minus Aenean veneror genitore nec umquam
esse satis potero, praestem licet omnia, gratus.
sentences.l: “May I look again upon Polyphemus and those jaws running with human blood, if any home, or the keel of the Ithacan, is more to me than this one; if I revere Aeneas less than my own father — and never shall I be able to be grateful enough, though I should render everything.
sentences.i: “Let me look on Polyphemus again, and on those jaws running with human blood, if ever a home, or the Ithacan's ship, means more to me than this one; if I honour Aeneas any less than my own father. And I shall never manage to be grateful enough, though I pay back everything I have.
sentences.n: This is an oath in the shape of a self-curse: the thing named first is the punishment invoked, and the si-clauses are what would earn it. adspiciam is ambiguous in form between the future indicative and the present subjunctive; the oath-shape wants the wishing subjunctive, and English has to say “may I”. Polyphemon and Aenean are Greek accusatives. rictus is the gaping open mouth of an animal, and fluidos with the ablative humano sanguine makes the blood run off it. hac is an ablative of comparison, “than this one” — the ship he is standing in; genitore is a second ablative of comparison, “than my father”. praestem licet omnia is concessive: licet with the subjunctive gives “though I should render everything”. gratus is held back to the very end of 171, with three words standing between it and the potero it belongs with. Magnus prints Ithaci, the genitive of Ithacus, “the Ithacan”, that is Ulysses; some editions print Ithace, which makes the island itself one of the things he might have preferred.

sentences.t:
Quod loquor et spiro caelumque et sidera solis
respicio, possimne ingratus et impius esse?
sentences.l: As for the fact that I speak and breathe and look back at the sky and the stars of the sun, could I be ungrateful and impious?
sentences.i: Given that I speak at all, and breathe, and look back at the sky and the sun's lights — could I be an ingrate and false to what I owe?
sentences.n: Quod at the head is the conjunction “as to the fact that”, laying down a state of affairs that the question then measures itself against. possimne is a potential subjunctive with the questioning -ne: “could I be”, not “am I”. impius is the negative of pietas, which is the whole duty owed to gods, parents and benefactors, so the word is heavier than English “impious”: to be impius here would be to fail Aeneas as a man fails a father. sidera solis, “the stars of the sun”, is an odd phrase however it is taken — the lights of the sky, sun and stars together, are what a man swallowed by the Cyclops would never have seen again. Magnus prints impius; some editions print inmemor, “forgetful”, which turns the charge from a failure of duty into a failure of memory.

sentences.t:
Ille dedit, quod non anima haec Cyclopis in ora
venit, et ut iam nunc lumen vitale relinquam,
aut tumulo aut certe non illa condar in alvo.
sentences.l: He gave it, that this breath of mine did not go into the Cyclops's jaws; and that, even if I give up the light of life this very moment, I shall be buried in a tomb, or at the least not in that belly.
sentences.i: It is his gift that this life of mine never went down the Cyclops's throat; and that, if I were to let go of the light of life this very minute, I should be buried in a tomb — or at any rate not in that belly.
sentences.n: dedit takes a quod-clause as its object, the same “the fact that” quod as in the line before, now the thing granted. anima is the breath that is the life, so what would have gone into the jaws is not the body but the life itself. ut here is concessive with the subjunctive relinquam, “even supposing I leave”, not a purpose clause: the sentence is not saying he was saved in order to die later. condar is future passive, “I shall be buried” — the form is also the present subjunctive, as adspiciam was at 168, but the aut ... aut wants a statement — and condere is the verb Latin uses both for laying a body in a tomb and for stowing food away; the pun is deliberate, and condebat comes back at 209 with in alvum, of the Cyclops packing limbs into his belly, against in alvo here.

sentences.t:
Quid mihi tunc animi (nisi si timor abstulit omnem
sensum animumque) fuit, cum vos petere alta relictus
aequora conspexi?
sentences.l: What of mind was there to me then — unless fear had carried off all sense and mind — when, left behind, I caught sight of you making for the deep waters?
sentences.i: What did I feel then — unless fear had stripped me of every sense and every feeling — when I saw you standing out for the open sea, and I left behind?
sentences.n: Quid animi is a partitive genitive, “what of mind”, and mihi ... fuit is a dative of possession: Latin says “what of feeling was to me” where English says “what did I feel”. nisi si is a doubled conditional, “unless, that is, if”, and the parenthesis takes the question back before it can be answered. vos petere ... aequora is an accusative and infinitive after conspexi, the ordinary way of reporting what one sees. relictus, one participle carrying everything that was done to him, is held to the end of 178, three words after the vos it is set against; and alta, the next word but one to the end of 178, is split from its own aequora at the head of 179 by that participle and the line-break.

sentences.t:
Volui inclamare, sed hosti
prodere me timui:
sentences.l: I wanted to cry out, but I was afraid to betray myself to the enemy:
sentences.i: I wanted to shout, but I was afraid of giving myself away to the enemy:
sentences.n: inclamare is to call out to someone — the shout that would have brought the ship back, and the same shout that would have brought the Cyclops. hosti is a dative with prodere, “betray to the enemy”. The two infinitives balance across the sentence in the same shape, inclamare on volui and prodere on timui, the wish against the fear. The colon after timui, early in 180, is Magnus's, and it makes what follows the reason for the fear.

sentences.t:
vestrae quoque clamor Ulixis
paene rati nocuit.
sentences.l: the shout of Ulysses too almost did harm to your ship.
sentences.i: even Ulysses' own shouting nearly brought disaster on your ship.
sentences.n: nocere takes a dative, so vestrae ... rati is “to your ship” rather than an object. ratis is properly a raft, and poets use it of any vessel. quoque here is the plain adverb “also” — worth checking each time, since the same letters can be quo-que, “and with which”. The shout meant is the taunt thrown back at the blinded giant from the departing ship, and what it brought after them is described in the lines immediately following.

sentences.t:
Vidi, cum monte revulsum
inmanem scopulum medias permisit in undas;
sentences.l: I saw, when he let fly a huge crag, torn from the mountain, into the middle of the waves;
sentences.i: I saw it, when he loosed a monstrous boulder, wrenched off the mountain, into the middle of the water;
sentences.n: Vidi stands with no object of its own: what he saw is the whole cum-clause that follows. The bare verb is then repeated at the head of 183, vidi iterum, so the two sights are set side by side by the repetition. monte is a bare ablative of separation with revulsum, “torn away from the mountain”, with no preposition. permisit is “let go, let fly”. medias ... in undas puts the adjective where English wants a noun: “into the middle of the waves”. inmanem is the edition's spelling and is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
vidi iterum veluti tormenti viribus acta
vasta Giganteo iaculantem saxa lacerto
et, ne deprimeret fluctus ventusve carinam,
pertimui, iam me non esse oblitus in illa.
sentences.l: I saw him again, hurling huge rocks with his Giant's arm as if they had been driven by the force of a siege-engine; and I was in dread lest wave or wind press the ship down, having by now forgotten that I was not on her.
sentences.i: A second time I saw him, slinging vast rocks with that giant arm as though a catapult had launched them; and I was in terror that wind or wave would drive the ship under — I had forgotten by now that I was not aboard her.
sentences.n: iaculantem is a participle standing as the object of vidi, “[him] hurling”: Latin sees the action, English has to put in a pronoun. acta is neuter plural and agrees with saxa, not with the thrower — it is the rocks that go as if an engine had sent them. tormentum is the twisted-rope artillery of a siege. lacertus is the upper arm and the muscle of it, and Giganteo makes the Cyclops one of the Giants. ne deprimeret is a fear clause after pertimui: Latin puts ne where English puts “that”, so the ne is not a negative here. oblitus is a deponent perfect participle, active in meaning — “having forgotten” — and it governs the accusative and infinitive me non esse in illa. The last clause, iam me non esse ... in illa, turns the whole terror into a joke against himself.

sentences.t:
Ut vero fuga vos a certa morte reduxit,
ille quidem totam gemebundus obambulat Aetnam
praetemptatque manu silvas et luminis orbus
rupibus incursat foedataque bracchia tabo
in mare protendens gentem exsecratur Achivam
atque ait:
sentences.l: But when flight had brought you back from certain death, he for his part, groaning, walks round the whole of Aetna and feels the woods ahead with his hand, and, robbed of his eye, blunders into the crags, and, stretching out into the sea his arms fouled with gore, curses the Achaean race, and says:
sentences.i: But once flight had carried you back out of certain death, he goes groaning round the whole of Aetna, feeling his way ahead through the woods with his hand, blundering into the crags now that his eye is gone; and holding out over the sea those arms of his, filthy with gore, he curses the whole Greek race, and says:
sentences.n: Ut with the perfect indicative reduxit is temporal, “when”, not final. The verbs then go over to the present — obambulat, praetemptat, incursat, exsecratur — and it is the tense change that makes the scene stand still while the escape is already over. obambulat takes totam Aetnam as a direct object of the ground covered. gemebundus belongs to a small class of adjectives in -bundus, “given to groaning”. orbus takes the genitive luminis, “robbed of his light”, lumen being the eye. praetemptat is the exact verb for feeling out the ground in front of you. tabum is the corrupt matter that runs from a wound, and foedata says it disfigures him: the blinding is still raw. exsecratur is deponent, active in meaning. Achivam is the poetic adjective for Achaean, Greek. Note that the sentence carries no terminal stop at all from 187 to the colon after ait in 192, six lines in one breath.

sentences.t:
“O si quis referat mihi casus Ulixem
aut aliquem e sociis, in quem mea saeviat ira,
viscera cuius edam, cuius viventia dextra
membra mea laniem, cuius mihi sanguis inundet
guttur et elisi trepident sub dentibus artus:
sentences.l: “O, if some chance should bring back Ulysses to me, or some one of his companions, against whom my anger might rage, whose innards I might eat, whose living limbs I might tear with my right hand, whose blood might flood my throat and whose crushed limbs might quiver under my teeth:
sentences.i: “Oh, if some accident would only hand Ulysses back to me, or any one of his crew — one for my rage to spend itself on, one whose guts I could eat, whose living limbs I could tear apart with my own hand, whose blood could pour down my throat, whose crushed limbs could twitch between my teeth:
sentences.n: si with the present subjunctive referat is an open wish, “if only chance would bring”. quis after si is the indefinite “some”, not the interrogative. Then come four relative clauses, three of them headed by cuius, and every verb in them is subjunctive — saeviat, edam, laniem, inundet, trepident. These are relative clauses of purpose or of characteristic: “someone for me to eat”, not “someone whom I eat”. The mood is what turns a description into a want, and English has to carry it with “might” or “could”. viscera is everything under the skin, flesh as well as guts. elisi is the participle of elidere, “to crush out”, so the limbs are crushed before they move, and trepidare is the verb for the small fast movement of a thing still alive. Everything in this unit is the Cyclops's own speech, quoted by Achaemenides inside his own account: it is a character's wish twice removed, never the poem speaking. The sentence runs five lines to the colon at the end of 196 with no stop inside it.

sentences.t: quam nullum aut leve sit damnum mihi lucis ademptae!”
sentences.l: how no loss at all, or how slight a one, the taking away of my light would be to me!”
sentences.i: how little a loss it would be to me — none at all, or next to none — that my sight was taken away!”
sentences.n: quam is exclamatory and sit is subjunctive: “how ... would it be”, kept hypothetical because the revenge has not happened. nullum aut leve is a correction downward in mid-sentence — he offers “no loss at all”, then settles for “a slight one”, which is the single flicker of restraint in the speech. damnum lucis ademptae is a genitive of definition: the loss that consists in the light's having been taken away. lux here is the eye and the daylight at once, as lumen was at 189.

sentences.t: Haec et plura ferox;
sentences.l: Such things and more, savage as he was;
sentences.i: That, and more of it, in his fury;
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is left out altogether: Latin can drop dixit and let the accusative Haec et plura stand by itself. ferox is a nominative adjective doing adverbial work, describing him while he speaks, and English has to turn it into a phrase. The semicolon then swings straight across to the listener: me is the first word after it.

sentences.t:
me luridus occupat horror
spectantem vultus etiamnum caede madentes
crudelesque manus et inanem luminis orbem
membraque et humano concretam sanguine barbam.
sentences.l: a livid horror takes hold of me as I look at his face still wet with slaughter, and his cruel hands, and the socket emptied of its eye, and his limbs, and his beard stiffened with human blood.
sentences.i: a horror that drained the colour out of me took hold as I stood looking at that face still wet with the killing, at the cruel hands, at the socket with no eye in it, at the limbs, at the beard caked stiff with human blood.
sentences.n: luridus properly describes the sallow colour of a frightened man, and Ovid gives it to the horror instead of to the man the horror seizes: the fear is named by the face it makes. occupat is a historic present, and spectantem agrees with me, hanging the whole catalogue on the one accusative. caedes is the killing and, by extension, the blood shed in it, so madentes says the face is wet with the act itself. At 189 the Cyclops was luminis orbus, robbed of his eye; here the same genitive luminis hangs on orbem, the round socket that is left. concretam is “curdled, grown solid”, the word for a liquid setting. Five objects are strung on spectantem — face, hands, socket, limbs, beard — and the list ends on the beard, which is what holds the blood longest.

sentences.t: mors erat ante oculos, minimum tamen ipsa doloris:
sentences.l: Death was before my eyes, yet death itself the least part of the pain:
sentences.i: Death was there in front of my eyes — and death itself was the smallest part of what I was suffering:
sentences.n: minimum ... doloris is a partitive genitive, “the least of pain”, and the second half of the line has no verb of its own: erat has to be carried across. ipsa is feminine and picks up mors, “death itself”. The colon promises what is worse than death, and the rest of the speech is that. Magnus prints ipsa doloris; some editions print illa malorum, “that the least of his troubles”, which spreads the comparison over misfortunes generally instead of pinning it to pain.

sentences.t:
et iam prensurum, iam nunc mea viscera rebar
in sua mersurum,
sentences.l: and I kept thinking that he was going to seize me, that this very moment he was going to sink my innards into his own,
sentences.i: and I kept thinking he was about to take hold of me, that any moment now he would bury my insides inside his own,
sentences.n: rebar is deponent and active in meaning, “I kept thinking”, and the imperfect makes it a thought held a long time rather than one that struck him once. prensurum and mersurum are both future infinitives with esse left out, which is ordinary in Latin and not a defect in the text. The object of prensurum is not expressed and English has to supply “me”; mea viscera is the object of mersurum alone. sua is reflexive to the Cyclops, so mea ... in sua sets the two sets of innards against each other using the one word for both.

sentences.t:
mentique haerebat imago
temporis illius, quo vidi bina meorum
ter quater adfligi sociorum corpora terrae,
cum super ipse iacens hirsuti more leonis
visceraque et carnes cumque albis ossa medullis
semianimesque artus avidam condebat in alvum.
sentences.l: and there clung to my mind the image of that time, in which I saw two bodies of my companions dashed three times, four times against the ground, while he himself, lying over them after the fashion of a shaggy lion, kept stowing innards and flesh and bones with their white marrow and half-living limbs into his greedy belly.
sentences.i: and the picture of that time stuck fast in my mind: when I watched a pair of my companions' bodies smashed against the ground three and four times over, and he himself, sprawled above them like a shaggy lion, packing away innards and flesh and bones with the white marrow in them and limbs still half alive into that greedy belly of his.
sentences.n: haerebat takes the dative menti, “was sticking to my mind” — the image is handled as a physical thing lodged there. bina is the distributive numeral, “two at a time, a pair”, not simply duo. ter quater, “three times, four times”, is a fixed idiom for repeated violence and counts the blows, not the bodies. adfligi is a passive infinitive after vidi, and English happens to have the same shape — “I saw the bodies dashed” — with terrae a dative, dashed against the ground. The word order of 205 and 206 is at its most tangled — five words stand between bina and the corpora it agrees with, and three between meorum and its sociorum. condebat is the same verb as condar at 176: there Achaemenides hoped to be laid in a tomb, here the Cyclops lays men in his belly, and Latin uses the one word for both. avidam belongs grammatically to alvum but describes the eater.

sentences.t: Me tremor invasit:
sentences.l: Trembling invaded me:
sentences.i: A fit of shaking came over me:
sentences.n: invadere is a verb of armed assault, so the trembling attacks him: Latin makes the bodily state the agent and the man its object. me stands first in the line and takes the blow.

sentences.t: stabam sine sanguine maestus;
sentences.l: I stood without blood, grieving;
sentences.i: I stood there drained of blood and stricken;
sentences.n: sine sanguine is literal and idiomatic at once — the blood has gone out of his face. The word sanguis has been doing hard work in this speech: it flooded the Cyclops's throat in his wish at 195 and caked his beard at 201, and here it is the blood that has left Achaemenides's own. maestus is another bare nominative adjective doing adverbial work, as ferox did at 198.

sentences.t:
mandentemque videns eiectantemque cruentas
ore dapes et frusta mero glomerata vomentem
talia fingebam misero mihi fata parari
sentences.l: and, seeing him chewing, and throwing bloody feasts back out of his mouth, and vomiting gobbets balled together with the unmixed wine, I kept imagining that such fates were being prepared for wretched me
sentences.i: and as I watched him chewing, and spitting the bloody meal back out of his mouth, and throwing up lumps of it clotted with raw wine, I kept picturing the same end being got ready for me, poor wretch
sentences.n: Three accusative participles hang on videns, all of them of the Cyclops — mandentem, eiectantem, and vomentem, the last pushed out to the end of 212. dapes is properly the food of a feast, and cruentas turns the feast-word against itself. merum is wine drunk unmixed with water, and glomerata is “rolled into a ball”. fingebam is “I kept shaping in my mind”, the verb for inventing something. talia ... fata parari is an accusative and infinitive with a passive infinitive: such fates were being prepared, and by whom is left unsaid. Note that the sentence ends here at parari with no stop printed on the page; what follows opens with perque, whose -que is the connective joining a new main clause, so the sense-unit ends where the punctuation does not.

sentences.t:
perque dies multos latitans omnemque tremescens
ad strepitum, mortemque timens cupidusque moriri,
glande famem pellens et mixta frondibus herba,
solus, inops, exspes, leto poenaeque relictus
hanc procul adspexi longo post tempore navem
oravique fugam gestu ad litusque cucurri —
sentences.l: and through many days, hiding, and trembling at every noise, fearing death and eager to die, driving hunger off with the acorn and with grass mixed among leaves, alone, resourceless, hopeless, left over to death and to punishment, I caught sight far off, after a long time, of this ship, and begged with a gesture for flight and ran down to the shore —
sentences.i: and through many days I hid, shaking at every sound, dreading death and longing to die, keeping hunger off with acorns and with grass and leaves together, alone, with nothing, with nothing to hope for, left over to death and to punishment — and then, after a long time, I saw this ship far out, and begged by a gesture to be taken off, and ran down to the shore —
sentences.n: The main verbs do not arrive until 218 and 219 — adspexi, oravi, cucurri — and everything before them is participles and adjectives piled on the one subject. mortemque timens cupidusque moriri sets the fear and the wish against each other inside a single line, 215. moriri is the old form of the infinitive of morior, where classical prose has mori. glande is a collective singular, “on the acorn”. solus, inops, exspes is three bare adjectives with no connective — asyndeton, doing the work of a pause. exspes is a rare word, simply “out of hope”. leto poenaeque relictus: relinquere with the dative is to leave a person over to a thing, and poena, punishment, says that being marooned was a sentence passed on him. The dash at the end of 219 is Magnus's own. This sentence runs six lines, from perque at 214 to that dash, with no terminal stop inside it.

sentences.t: et movi.
sentences.l: and I moved them.
sentences.n: movi is given no object at all: the men he was signalling to are left to be supplied, and movere is the verb for moving somebody to pity. The brevity is the whole effect — the six lines before this took him from many days of hiding to the shore, and the result of it takes two words.

sentences.t: Graiumque ratis Troiana recepit!
sentences.l: and a Trojan vessel received a Greek!
sentences.i: and a Greek — a Trojan ship took him in!
sentences.n: Four words, and the point of them is the order: Graium first, then ratis Troiana, so that the Greek and the Trojan ship stand side by side with only the noun ratis between the two national words. Latin can make the contrast by position alone where English has to reach for a “yet” or a dash. Graium is the same accusative singular that Macareus used at the end of 163, when he asked why a barbarian prow was carrying a Greek; the question and its answer use the one word. recipere is the verb for taking a person in, giving refuge.

sentences.t:
Tu quoque pande tuos, comitum gratissime, casus
et ducis et turbae, quae tecum est credita ponto.”
sentences.l: You too, most welcome of companions, spread open your own fortunes, and those of your leader and of the crowd that was entrusted with you to the sea.”
sentences.i: Now tell me your own story in turn, dearest of my companions — yours, and your leader's, and that of the company that was put to sea along with you.”
sentences.n: pande is “spread open”, the verb for unrolling a book or opening up a country, and Latin uses it of telling a story out at length. tuos ... casus is split around the vocative comitum gratissime, so the address falls inside the phrase it interrupts. casus is the same noun Macareus used at 162 of the chance that had saved Achaemenides; here it is “the things that befell you”. gratissime is the superlative of gratus, and gratus was Achaemenides's own word at 171 for the gratitude he could never sufficiently show — it comes back as his name for the man he is talking to, the one word covering both being grateful and being welcome. credita takes the dative ponto, “entrusted to the sea”, which is the standing way of saying “put to sea” and keeps the sense of a thing handed over on trust. quoque here is the plain adverb, “you too”.
